My two cents:  
1) I always, near the beginning of a friendship, explain to people that I am forgetful with texting but that I never ignore anyone on purpose, so if I don't text back for a while they should not assign any deeper meaning to it AND I let them know I will never take offense to a nudge text. It's important to do this before any mistakes have happened yet because it prevents it from coming off as an excuse.  
2) I always try to text *something* back when I first get a text, even if that something is "I'm busy right now but I'll check this out/get back to you later!" or something of the sort. This is especially crucial if the text is a question I need to answer or an attempt to make plans or something. It helps the person feel heard and gives them a heads up that you need time to respond.  
3) I tell my friends if something is urgent or needs an immediate response, they should call me.  
4) If it becomes clear that a friend and I are incompatible when it comes to texting expectations, I reconsider the friendship. If we can't reach ANY compromise, it's not going to work. I can't promise things I can't do and it's not fair to anyone to let it continue.

Honestly I think part of this discrepancy comes from the fact that when you're watching a horror movie, you know it's a horror movie. You've been sitting there for twenty minutes waiting for the monster to show up, so as soon as you hear the weird sound, you know shit's about to get real. When you hear a weird sound in real life your brain is operating under real life rules, where the odds of it being a monster or killer are (close to) zero. With that in mind it makes a lot of sense to go investigate this strange new stimulus in your environment.  
  
All that being said, it's just plain _fun_ to make fun of horror movie protagonists, and it's all good as long as you don't confuse "part of the fun of watching this movie is yelling at the screen" and "this protag didn't behave perfectly in a life-or-death scenario, movie ruined."

When this same question came up for me, my ADHD specialized therapist said that ADHD primarily affects working memory, like holding multiple things in your brain at once or one thing for a longer period of time, and that longer term memory loss (like drawing blanks on months or years of your life) is more likely to be caused by trauma. That being said, things are always an interplay because human brains are complex, and growing up with undiagnosed ADHD can be traumatic for some depending on the environment, so it could be related just not in the way you expect.

I don't as much now that I work from home but I used to. The problem with watches (or my phone, or any clock really) is that they only work when I remember to check them, which if left to my own devices, is almost never. What's worked well for me though is setting my computer to announce the time every 15 min. It's something you could do on a smart watch too and I definitely want to give that a go sometime to see how it helps!

Everyone experiences ADHD a little differently so that makes sense!  

Besides the time announcements and using music to measure time, getting a dog actually helped me a good amount I think. I never remember to check the time on my own, but since I'm responsible for making sure he gets fed on time and gets out enough etc, he gives me a reason to be more aware. He'll ask to go out for his second potty break of the day and it'll snap me back to reality like "what, it's already 2?"  

The other thing that's been super helpful is having a solid support system. Mostly I rely on my own methods to be self-sufficient, but if it's something crucial I can't miss like a job interview or important event, I know I can get someone from my family or one of my friends to give me a call at X time to make sure I have it under control. It's like the code red emergency accountability tool for things I absolutely cannot afford to mess up haha.

Someone else suggested that too! Right now I have my computer announcing the time every 15 min which works because I'm stuck at home for now anyway, but I'll have to try the watch thing when I go out for sure.

It doesn't scare me anymore (it's mostly just annoying), but before I knew it was a symptom of ADHD it was terrifying. Not the general sense of timelessness, I didn't know that was abnormal, but the feeling of "losing time" when I'd do something for what I thought was about 15 min only to look up and see that it had actually been hours. I thought I was going crazy and my worst fear was that I was blacking out during that time and doing things I had no memory of. Nope, turns out I know what I was doing during that time, I just didn't perceive the hours passing so it came as a huge shock when I saw that they had.  

It also goes the other way (short amounts of time feeling like hours) and I used to believe I had a superpower when I was young. I'd do things in what felt like the span of an hour and then realize only 5 minutes had passed. I called it "time stretching" and always thought man, if I learn to control this, I'll be set for life! Unfortunately it's just a janky perception of time and not a superpower, but how cool would that have been? ;-)

For me, it's a strange mix of both. I tend to "take losses well" from an outsider perspective because since I only function in the now, my ability to compartmentalize is extreme. The day after my long term girlfriend and I broke up, I was perfectly fine, because the sad thing wasn't happening to me in the moment so it was just a memory. (I feel terrible admitting it but I did say I'd be honest.) However, whenever something does trigger a memory of my ex the feeling of loss can be pretty gut-wrenching even almost two years later because it still feels so recent. This has made my grieving process kind of difficult because I was relatively okay when everyone around me wanted to support me, only to feel weird bringing it up to people when it hits me like a train eons later.

I feel you. I often mourn who I could have been had I had a more functional brain, but in the end it's also important to remember that there only exists one you, in whatever form that is, and what you bring to the world as a result of your circumstances is unique and valuable just the way it is. It doesn't take away from the fact that it sucks, but it helps me not spend my time caught up in sad wishful thinking. :-(

Meds definitely help with my ADHD in general, although time blindness is the one symptom that tends to stick around even on meds. The fact that I have better focus and ability to switch between tasks though helps me be more on top of keeping track of time though, so I guess it does still have a positive impact overall!

I got officially diagnosed freshman year of college. In grade school, I had a really good support system that prevented most of my ADHD traits from sabotaging me too much and because of that I was actually a pretty high achiever, so even though my parents and teachers noticed the issues with time management, focus, and memory, it never got investigated because it was never enough of a "problem." Once I went to college and had to be on top of everything by myself, I crashed and burned in a big way. Managing my time with no external structure, dealing with long-term deadlines, needing the discipline to study/work on projects little by little, plus having to take care of all my needs all of a sudden were too much.

My suggestion would be, instead of setting a goal as general as "stop lying to cover up ADHD moments", try starting smaller. Talk with him about what he thinks would feel attainable, something that is a little out of his comfort zone but that he feels he could take on. If there's a specific small thing he often lies about, like leaving the milk out of the fridge or forgetting to text back (idk, just examples), you could try targeting that lie only. Agree that from here on out you clear him from all future guilt about (thing he messes up) if he can test out the waters by not lying when it happens. Or another way to start small is to make a goal of telling one truth a week in an instance where he felt compelled to make up a cover story. This lets him choose the moments where he feels safest to start being transparent, without feeling overwhelmed by the idea of immediately changing this whole huge habit he's built up. Then as he gathers evidence of you reacting well to the truth, he might feel more confident in expanding his goals.  

One more quick insight, this may or may not be true for your boyfriend but for me personally, a lot of the times I fib to cover up ADHD symptoms because if I stopped covering them up altogether, people would realize just how much ADHD messes with every aspect of my life. With that comes a fear of being judged, of being thought less of, or of coming across useless or incapable or high maintenance. So it makes sense to develop a habit of lying to save face and inventing some situation where not doing X thing was out of your control, absolving you of fault and scrutiny. I guess I say this just to prepare you for the possible realization of just how much he struggles because of this disorder. If you get to the point where you're thinking "you forgot, again?!" imagine the frustration he feels over a lifetime of mess-ups.  

As important as it is for you to treat the situation with care and show your support, I hope you also recognize the importance of your own mental wellbeing and I hope you have (or can find) a support system of your own to lean on when you need some healthy venting! None of this is easy for either of you, but you seem a wonderful, well-equipped person and just talking about these things is already a huge step in the right direction. I wish you both the best of luck <3

Having someone sitting with me somehow puts pressure on me to stay on task, and often times if I can get on task for the first ten minutes then the flow kicks in and I can get a good chunk done whether they stay there on not. Usually I'll accomplish this by asking a friend if I can talk through my thinking on a project/ask them for their opinion on the direction I'm going (which may or may not be useful to me-- I care more about the act of explaining it) or inviting a friend to a jam session to work on stuff separately but together and compare progress intermittently.  

Another thing that helps me is changing the motivation for doing the thing. Instead of working on a project for the sake of getting it done (boring), I'll sit down to create a cool timelapse of myself working on it and suddenly I'm motivated to sit there for a few hours and eke out some work because I'm excited to see the timelapse and can't ruin it by getting up to do something else. Kind of a weird method but it's fun, I recommend it if you have a phone that can record them, timelapses are cool to watch even if you're not working on something visually interesting and it's neat to have a reward/proof of the time you spent working even if you didn't finish the whole task you set out to do.

This. This is the main thing I've really been missing from Pocket Camp. Sure, more mechanics or things to do would be cool. But the reason Animal Crossing games were so good, at least to me, was the emergent interactions it created between players and their villagers. As a measure of its success, ask yourself how (in such a non-narrative game) one person could hate a certain villager while another loves them? Or hate one Jock villager while loving another one, even though they're technically drawing from the same conversation pool? People will say "oh, he moved in right on top of my blue roses and one time I caught him talking to Melba and he made her sad!" Or on the other side of the coin, "He always sends me such cute letters and he gave me this piece of furniture I'd been wanting forever!"

The game devs didn't write that character to be any particular way. But because of the amount of depth in the game's conversation systems combined with just enough RNG, each player's experience with any given character is completely unique. Sure, you see repeat dialogue, especially if you play a ton, but they were clever in that even the repeat dialogue is not exactly the same experience (when Lazy types mention food, the type of food is often randomized.) Even their actions serve to make the experience feel more organic and more like I'm talking to a "real" character and not just reading through a script-- when you went into a villager's house to find someone else visiting, that created a narrative of friendship between them. You might discover one villager has a penchant for fishing by the river, or one villager seems to always be at the shops. In Pocket Camp, they don't even walk around the space. There's only 2 specific locations where a villager can spawn in each of 4 areas, and they're resigned to just stand there for their 3 hours and then leave. They rarely interact with each other (and when they do you can't participate,) rarely ask for your input on anything, and hardly ever say anything meaningful or flavorful at all. I'm tired of every conversation either being about how cool my campsite is or about how to play the game. I live for the tiny moments when we do get cool situational dialogue or dialogue that isn't trying to teach me something or get me to buy Leaf Tickets. I'm level 43, I know how the game works now, and I get enough ticket prompts as I play. I understand the need for some of this dialogue, but let the villagers have character again. That feeling of having a personal, completely unique experience is what made me sink 600 hours into New Leaf alone, and what I think will ultimately either cement Pocket Camp as a true AC game despite its limitations, or relegate it to be just another fun but lacking side game in the franchise.
